title: HEG Neurofeedback
subtitle: Feedback based on cortical blood-flow or oxygenation signals
altText: Chalkboard-style clinical diagram illustrating heg neurofeedback within a neurofeedback closed loop.
learningObjectives: Explain heg neurofeedback without diagnostic overreach.
Distinguish measurement, mechanism and clinical outcome in heg neurofeedback.
Identify one safety or validity limitation relevant to heg neurofeedback.

sections.explainSimply: HEG uses near-infrared or thermal measures related to haemodynamic activity rather than electrical EEG rhythms.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Haemodynamic signals are slower and affected by systemic physiology, movement, scalp blood flow and device characteristics.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: HEG is a distinct modality and should not be presented as interchangeable with EEG neurofeedback. Evidence is limited and heterogeneous.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Choosing a camera lens: every method emphasises some information and introduces its own distortions.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need to understand heg neurofeedback to evaluate mechanism claims, informed consent, treatment fit and whether change transfers to real-world function.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Breathing and skin temperature can influence the signal.
sections.clinicalPearl: The trained metric is an intermediate target; the clinical endpoint is meaningful function.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician using heg neurofeedback predefines the target, checks raw signal and artifacts, monitors symptoms and function, and reviews whether change generalises beyond the feedback display.
sections.limitationsCautions: Breathing and skin temperature can influence the signal. Evidence classification: emerging; insufficient clinical evidence.
